question: According to the Commission, the AI Omnibus entered into force on 27 July 2026. The rules on high-risk systems set out in Annex III will apply from 2 December 2027 and from 2 August 2028 for the respective systems that have been integrated into products. Clear information is needed on the aspects that are already in place to protect citizens and what will come into force later on.

It is therefore considered necessary to provide practical guidance for the human review of adverse decisions. The human review should be carried out by trained officials who are best placed to reject an algorithmic recommendation.

Before public authorities use such systems, I would suggest establishing common standards for independent checks and publishing a brief risk assessment that is easy to understand, with personal data protection. Small and medium-sized businesses need easy-to-use compliance tools. Likewise, providers must provide sufficient documentation and not pass their responsibilities on to small users in a non-transparent way.
In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
When will uniform practical guidance be given on reporting, human review and explaining decisions, depending on the applicable regime?
How are citizens affected by the systems in Annex III protected during the transition period?
What tools will be given to SMEs to exercise compliance and check the documentation of their suppliers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.11.2026) While the AI Omnibus postponed the application of the AI Act’s1 Annex III high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 and the Annex I, point a, high-risk rules to 2 August 2028, natural persons remain protected by existing applicable EU and national legislation, including data protection, non-discrimination, consumer protection, employment and product safety rules.

The AI Act’s already applicable prohibitions, transparency obligations and general-purpose AI rules provide additional safeguards during this period2. Human oversight is regulated by Articles 14 and 26 of the AI Act and is addressed through guidelines on high-risk requirements and deployer obligations, both of which are currently in the process of being drafted by the AI Office.

The right to an explanation in relation to AIassisted decisions will also be covered by the guidelines on deployer obligations. Reporting related to serious incidents is regulated by Articles 73 and 26(5) of the AI Act, for which draft guidelines and a reporting template have been published for consultation3.

The AI Office supports small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) through the AI Act Service Desk and Single Information Platform4. Guidelines, templates, standards and AI Pact webinars provide further practical compliance support5. For SMEs integrating general-purpose AI models, the Code of Practice’s model documentation form provides a useful reference for reviewing information supplied by model providers6.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council laying down harmonised rules on

artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act). 2 See AI Act’s Article 5 on prohibitions, Article 50 on transparency, and Article 51-55 on general-purpose AI rules. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/consultations/ai-act-commission-issues-draft-guidance-and-reportingtemplate-serious-ai-incidents-and-seeks. 4 https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en. 5 https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/resources. 6 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai.
